title: Final Expense Pay Per Call: How It Works
h1: Final expense pay per call: how it works and how to run it
description: How final expense pay per call works: who buys the calls, what makes a call billable, the routing rules buyers expect and how to protect your margin.
faq: What is final expense pay per call?

It is a way of selling inbound calls from people interested in final expense or burial insurance. Publishers and affiliates generate the calls and insurance agencies or call centers pay for calls that meet agreed rules.
What makes a final expense call billable?
Usually a minimum call length, a caller in a state where the agent is licensed, a call during agent hours and a caller who has not already been sold to that buyer. Each buyer sets its own rules.
Is final expense pay per call compliant?

It depends on how the traffic is generated, the states involved and the consent collected. Tools such as recording notices, do-not-call list handling and repeat-caller blocks help, but you should confirm your obligations with your own counsel.
body:
Final expense pay per call is the sale of inbound phone calls from people looking for final expense or burial insurance. A publisher or affiliate generates the caller, the call is routed to a licensed agent or agency that can help, and the buyer pays only when the call meets agreed rules, usually a minimum length, an allowed state and agent hours. It is one of the most common insurance verticals in pay per call because the product is often sold on the phone in a single conversation.

Who buys final expense calls

  • Independent agencies with licensed agents who sell final expense policies over the phone.
  • Insurance call centers that take high call volume across many states.
  • Networks and marketplaces that buy calls and resell them to agencies.

Each buyer sets its own price, states, hours and daily cap, so the same caller can be worth very different amounts to different buyers.

What makes a final expense call billable

Before you send a single call, agree in writing what the buyer will pay for. Common rules include:

  • Minimum call duration, measured from when the agent picks up.
  • Licensed states only: a call from a state the agent cannot write in is wasted for everyone.
  • Agent hours: calls outside opening hours are not answered and not paid.
  • No duplicates: the same caller is not sold to the same buyer twice within an agreed window.
  • Daily caps: once a buyer reaches its limit, further calls must go elsewhere.

How to route final expense calls

Waterfall routing

With a waterfall, calls try buyers in a fixed order and move on when one is closed, capped or does not answer. It suits fixed agreements with a small number of agencies.

Real-time bidding

When several agencies want the same callers, real-time call bidding asks every eligible buyer for a price at the same moment and sends the call to the highest bid above your minimum. If nobody bids, the call falls back to your waterfall. Our explainer on how real-time call bidding works covers the mechanics.

Check the rules first

Whichever method you use, the caller's state, the buyer's hours and caps and repeat-caller rules should be checked before the call rings, not after the buyer disputes it.

Protecting your margin

Final expense margins depend heavily on how many calls turn out billable. If you pay a traffic source for every call but buyers only pay for calls that pass their rules, short and duplicate calls eat your profit. Three habits help:

  1. Grade every traffic source on real call history and pause sources sending too many short calls.
  2. Pay each affiliate their own rate, so stronger sources can earn more without raising everyone's payout.
  3. Review recordings and transcripts when a buyer questions a call, so disputes are settled with facts.

Use the pay per call profit calculator to see how your billable rate, buyer payout and affiliate payout change your monthly profit.

Compliance basics

Insurance calls carry extra rules around consent, call recording and do-not-call lists, and they vary by state and by how traffic is generated.
